profile.reading:
This Lumen colocation facility, internally identified in public records as Madison 1, is located at 612 West Main Street, Madison, WI 53715, in Dane County; Lumen does not publish individual building addresses or specs on its own site for any of its 175-plus North American colocation sites. Lumen Technologies, formerly CenturyLink (renamed Lumen on September 14, 2020, with its stock ticker changing from CTL to LUMN on September 18, 2020) and built in part on CenturyLink's November 1, 2017 acquisition of Level 3 Communications, operates this facility as part of a network-centric edge colocation product rather than a wholesale hyperscale campus. Lumen's own colocation data sheet states more than 175 carrier-neutral data centers across more than 60 North American markets, offering cabinet power in the 3 to 15 kilowatt range described as varying by site; unlike the wholesale operators tracked elsewhere in this registry, Lumen does not disclose per-building square footage or total MW capacity for any of its sites.

The Wisconsin Public Service Commission, headquartered in Madison, overhauled We Energies' data center tariff on April 24, 2026 after a year-long review, lowering the qualifying demand threshold from 500 to 100 megawatts, extending the minimum contract term to 15 years, and eliminating a capacity-only billing option that would have let large data centers pay just 75% of generation costs, now requiring 100% cost responsibility instead. We Energies separately announced plans in November 2025 to add nearly 3 gigawatts of new solar, battery, and gas capacity to meet data-center-driven demand in southeastern Wisconsin, with Madison Gas and Electric acquiring a 10% stake in five of the associated solar projects, a more than $2.5 billion investment.

Madison's data center footprint is modest compared to southeastern Wisconsin's Mount Pleasant/Kenosha corridor, where Microsoft's much larger hyperscale campus has driven most of the state's recent utility-scale grid planning, giving this downtown building a smaller, network-edge role by comparison.

reading.body:
Lumen Madison 1 is a downtown colocation facility operated as part of a 175-plus-site edge network rather than a wholesale hyperscale campus. Lumen does not publish power capacity, square footage, or density for any individual site, disclosing only a company-wide cabinet power range of 3 to 15 kilowatts per site that varies by location. Without published specifications, the facility's scale relative to AI infrastructure buildout cannot be determined from available data.

Wisconsin's regulatory environment for data centers shifted sharply in April 2026 when the Public Service Commission lowered We Energies' qualifying demand threshold from 500 to 100 megawatts and eliminated a reduced-rate option, now requiring full generation cost responsibility. We Energies simultaneously announced nearly 3 gigawatts of planned new solar, battery, and gas capacity to serve data-center-driven demand in southeastern Wisconsin, though Madison's colocation footprint remains modest compared to Microsoft's hyperscale campus in the Mount Pleasant and Kenosha corridor where most of the state's recent utility-scale grid planning has concentrated.

Among Wisconsin's six mapped facilities, only one has published megawatt capacity on record. Lumen Madison 1 ranks second in the state by published capacity but publishes no capacity figure, meaning the rank reflects an absence of disclosed data rather than measured capability relative to AI scaling needs.
